newsitem.title: JAPAN: HK firm's listing to boost Tokyo bourse's profile. [CORRECTED 10:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: HK firm's listing to boost Tokyo bourse's profile. [CORRECTED 10:00 GMT]

text.p: The listing in Tokyo this week of Hong Kong property developer Henderson Land will boost the market's international profile and may lead more Asian firms to seek listing here, analysts say.

But unless Japanese financial deregulation gets into full swing, stock authorities are going to find it difficult to entice more Asian companies to list in Tokyo and Osaka, which have suffered from a spate of foreign delistings, they say.
"It (Henderson Land) is a perfect issue," said a major securities house broker for foreign stocks in Japan.
"With people expecting a hard time for about half a year from now in Japan, new China-related issues should gain the attention of investors," he said.

Henderson Land Development Co Ltd, a major property developer based in Hong Kong with interests in the British colony and China, will issue 33 million new shares as part of a secondary listing in Tokyo. Dealing begins on Wednesday.

"With foreign companies leaving Japan, it (Henderson's listing) is certainly good news. The TSE (Tokyo Stock Exchange) and OSE (Osaka Securities Exchange) are gearing up to invite new foreign issues, especially Asian issues," said Shinichi Ichikawa, a strategist at Credit Lyonnais Securities.

Late last year, the Osaka bourse set up an Asian stock section targeting medium-sized companies from Asia. The head of Tokyo bourse went to China to urge companies there to consider Tokyo instead of other major international markets for listing.
But Ichikawa said unless the Tokyo and Osaka exchanges step up restructuring efforts and lower their costs, the bourses may not be able to prevent more foreign firms from leaving.
In the last five years, 61 foreign firms have delisted from the TSE, while only three firms have come in, according to TSE data. (TSE corrects number of foreign firms de-listed).

In November, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled a five-year "Big Bang" plan to deregulate Japan's financial markets, which for now is focused on liberalising brokerage fees and tearing down barriers among the banking, broking and insurance sectors.
Despite the increasing attractiveness of Asian stocks as economies in the region boom, analysts say their listings will not necessarily enliven foreign stock trading in Japan.
"Even if the issue (of Henderson Land) is not listed on the TSE, institutional investors who are interested in the issue will buy it anyway in Hong Kong," Ichikawa said.
"Regardless of Henderson Land's listing in Tokyo, we are pretty much focused in Asian markets (for Asian shares)," said a fund manager at a Japanese life insurance company.
"In fact, we have increased our weighting of shares in markets there for the past three or four years," he said.
Asian markets are Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, as well as Hong Kong and China, he said.

Henderson Land will be the second Asian issue to list in Tokyo after Malaysian infrastructure developer YTL Corp Bhd did so a year ago. YTL's current share price of 660 yen in Tokyo is near its record high of 680 yen.
Other Asian firms are expected to tap the Tokyo market.

The Japanese financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun has reported that South Korea's Samsung Group plans to merge units of two of its member firms in Japan by the year-end and list shares of the merged firm on the TSE. But Samsung said a decision on such a listing had yet to be finalised.
Media reports have said two Chinese firms are also likely to list on the TSE this year following moves by Japan and China to promote information exchanges. ($1=121 yen)
